title: Indrajit's arrows
hook: a warrior nobody can see, arrows from an empty sky, and the brothers fall

segments.voice: Yesterday: the siege. Four gates surrounded, Angada carrying one last offer of peace — your line, peace offered, even at the gates — and then the battle began. Did you make a plain offer of peace somewhere? Today, the first night of the war, and Ravana's son. Day six hundred forty-one.

The first day of fighting goes badly for Lanka. Duel after duel, the monkey and bear leaders win, and the rakshasa champions fall or run. The sun sets, and the fighting goes on in the dark, by the light of weapons. In one of those duels, Angada smashes the chariot of Ravana's son, killing his horses and driver. The prince jumps clear. And then he does something the monkeys have no answer for. He disappears.
screen: `A GOOD FIRST DAY.` → `FIGHTING IN THE DARK.` → `HE DISAPPEARS.`

segments.voice: His name is Indrajit, Ravana's son. It means conqueror of Indra, the king of the gods, and the epic says he earned it: he once fought Indra and carried him off as a captive. His birth name was Meghanada, the one who roars like a thundercloud. Now he rises out of sight, up among the clouds, and from there he starts shooting. The arrows come out of an empty sky. Nobody can tell where to aim back. And these aren't ordinary arrows. Valmiki says they turn into serpents as they strike, and they wrap around Rama and Lakshmana, binding them tight. Snake after snake, arrow after arrow, until the two brothers can't move. They fall, side by side, on the battlefield, covered in shafts like a bed of arrows. The monkey army gathers around them, stunned. Sugriva, Angada, Hanuman, Jambavan, all staring at the two men they came to fight for, lying still. Indrajit, invisible, shouts down that he's killed them, and goes home to tell his father. What makes this frightening isn't only the power. It's that you can't see where it comes from. A blow you can see, you can dodge. A blow from nowhere makes everything feel unsafe. Valmiki lets the reader feel that for a while. He doesn't rush to the rescue. The first night of the war ends with the heroes down, and the sky quiet, and nobody sure whether they're alive.
screen: `INDRAJIT: CONQUEROR OF INDRA.` · `ARROWS FROM AN EMPTY SKY.` · `ARROWS THAT TURN INTO SERPENTS.` · `THE BROTHERS FALL.` · then, large: `A BLOW FROM NOWHERE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath be slow and low in the belly. Think of something that has hit you lately from nowhere: worry with no clear source, a mood that arrived uninvited, bad news out of a quiet sky. Don't chase where it came from. Just notice where you feel it in the body, the way you'd notice a cord wrapped around your arm. Breathe into that place. Let it loosen one turn. The bell holds the time.
Indrajit's arrows. Shot by Ravana's son from out of sight, they turn into serpents and bind Rama and Lakshmana, and the brothers fall.
Your line: a blow from nowhere. Today, when a worry hits from nowhere, find where it sits in the body before you fight it. Day six hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Ramayana tellers often slow down at the serpent-arrows, the nāgapāśa, letting listeners sit with the heroes' fall before the rescue comes.

match.prompt: the first night — tap the pairs.

myth: Indrajit fights Rama face to face
he rises out of sight and shoots from the clouds.
Indrajit's name means conqueror of Indra
he once defeated Indra, the king of the gods.
the first night ends with Rama and Lakshmana bound and fallen
Valmiki leaves them there before any rescue comes.

fork.setup: you're Indrajit. your chariot is smashed and the monkeys are winning the night. what do you do?
options: vanish into the sky and shoot from there.
fork.reveal: he becomes invisible and rains serpent-arrows from the clouds, binding Rama and Lakshmana.

original.note: Sanskrit nāgapāśa: the serpent noose, from nāga, serpent, and pāśa, noose or snare.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rama and Lakshmana were wounded by ordinary arrows.
what it means: Indrajit's arrows became serpents that bound them, shot by a warrior no one could see.
what a scholar hears: the Uttara Kanda tells how Meghanada won the name Indrajit by capturing Indra himself.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 43–45 (the night battle; Angada and Indrajit; the serpent-arrows)
Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (Meghanada defeats Indra and is named Indrajit)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
Angada smashing Indrajit's chariot, horses and charioteer in the night battle: confirm.
Indrajit as Ravana's eldest son, and his birth name Meghanada: confirm.
The Uttara Kanda's account of Indrajit capturing Indra: cited by book only; add the sarga.
Indrajit's announcement of the brothers' death to Ravana is placed here briefly; day 642 picks up from it.
